missingAwards.step: The Loss Distribution Is Not the Audit Report
missingAwards.statement: The bug classes that get the most audit attention are not the ones that lose the most money.

missingAwards.step: The Six Archetypes That Explain the Wreckage
missingAwards.statement: Most catastrophic on-chain losses are one of six recurring shapes — learn the shapes and you can triage any new incident in minutes.

missingAwards.step: First Dollar of Security
missingAwards.statement: A finite security budget spent on the most interesting risk instead of the largest one is a subsidy to the attacker.

missingAwards.step: MEV Is an Adversary, Not a Fee
missingAwards.statement: The order of transactions is itself a resource, and someone is extracting value from yours whether or not you modeled them.

missingAwards.step: Build the Loss-Cause Ledger for a Real Protocol
missingAwards.statement: A threat model you cannot map to real historical losses is a fantasy; ground it in the ledger or discard it.

missingAwards.step: Say the Number to the Board
missingAwards.statement: A board does not fund fear; it funds a defensible range of probable loss against a defensible cost of control.

missingAwards.step: Reentrancy Has Four Doors, Not One
missingAwards.statement: The checks-effects-interactions rule stops the classic attack and none of its three modern relatives.

missingAwards.step: Spot Price Is Not a Price
missingAwards.statement: A price you can move within a single transaction is not an oracle; it is an attacker-controlled input.

missingAwards.step: Break It, Then Guard It, in Foundry
missingAwards.statement: You do not understand a vulnerability until you have written the exploit that proves it and the test that proves the fix.

missingAwards.step: Access Control, Proxy Slots, and the Signature You Can Replay
missingAwards.statement: The quiet bugs — a missing modifier, a colliding storage slot, a domain separator left off — move more money than the loud ones.

missingAwards.step: Two Findings, One Night Left
missingAwards.statement: The elegant bug that skims dust is a trap when a boring bug can empty the contract.

missingAwards.step: Invariants That Break the Contract Before the Attacker Does
missingAwards.statement: A unit test checks the case you imagined; an invariant test lets the machine imagine the case you missed.

missingAwards.step: An Audit Is a Search, Not a Certificate
missingAwards.statement: The word audited on a landing page has killed more protocols than any single bug.

missingAwards.step: The Pipeline: Static, Fuzz, Differential
missingAwards.statement: Each tool sees a different class of bug; running one and calling it coverage is theater.

missingAwards.step: When Fuzzing Stops and Proof Begins
missingAwards.statement: Fuzzing finds bugs; formal verification proves their absence within a spec — and the spec is where all the difficulty moves.

missingAwards.step: The Sign-Off They Want You to Give
missingAwards.statement: The most dangerous line in an audit is the clean summary on a system whose real risk you were told not to look at.

missingAwards.step: Run a Real Review on Live Code
missingAwards.statement: The proof you can review is a report on code you did not write, with findings someone could act on.

missingAwards.step: Designing a Bounty That Attracts the Right Hacker
missingAwards.statement: A bug bounty is a market you design; price it wrong and the best researchers sell your Critical to someone else.

missingAwards.step: The Key Is the Asset
missingAwards.statement: On-chain there is no account recovery, no chargeback, and no fraud department — the key is the money.

missingAwards.step: Safe Multisig, MPC, and the Delegatecall Foot-Gun
missingAwards.statement: A multisig only protects you if each signer can independently see and refuse what they are signing.

missingAwards.step: The Screen Says It Is Fine
missingAwards.statement: Every catastrophic multisig loss shares one moment: a competent signer approved a transaction they could not actually read.

missingAwards.step: Verify the Hash Before You Sign It
missingAwards.statement: If you cannot independently reproduce the hash your device is asking you to sign, you are blind signing no matter how good your hardware is.

missingAwards.step: Exchange-Grade Custody and the Insider You Cannot Audit
missingAwards.statement: Hot, warm, and cold segmentation stops the outside attacker; only dual control and least privilege stop the one you hired.

missingAwards.step: The Emergency Withdrawal Outside the Allowlist
missingAwards.statement: The controls that matter are the ones that hold when a powerful person, under real urgency, asks you to skip them.

missingAwards.step: Containment When There Is No Undo
missingAwards.statement: On-chain you cannot reverse the theft, so incident response is entirely about bounding what has not happened yet.

missingAwards.step: Capturing a Protocol Through Its Own Rules
missingAwards.statement: Governance is executable code with the highest privileges in the system, and every defense against capturing it trades decentralization for safety.

missingAwards.step: A Treasury That Governs Itself: The Masternode Model
missingAwards.statement: A DAO treasury's real security control is not the smart contract but the humans who read every proposal before it can spend.

missingAwards.step: The Pause Key While the Funds Drain
missingAwards.statement: The moment you most need to act decisively is the moment your community's principles most demand you do not.

missingAwards.step: The War Room: Board, Community, and the Attacker
missingAwards.statement: During a live incident you are running three negotiations at once, and silence in any of them is a decision with consequences.

missingAwards.step: Write the On-Chain Incident Runbook Before You Need It
missingAwards.statement: The plan you write calmly today is the only thing that will function when the treasury is draining and you have sixty seconds.
